conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this visit. I’m Dr. Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived.

We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up during the first year postpartum. It also includes a question about thoughts of self-harm, so if anything feels too heavy today we can pause or shift gears at any time.

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you plan to hurt yourself or someone else, or if there’s concern about a child’s safety. I’ll ask each question conversationally—no clipboard, no judgment—and we’ll go at your pace. When we’re done I’ll add up the numbers privately and we’ll talk about what the score means and any next steps that might help you feel more like yourself again.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has it been mostly easy, sometimes, not often, or not at all?

*shifts a little in the chair, eyes flicking down to my hands*

I... um... I can still laugh, I guess. Sometimes? Like, when my husband sends those silly memes or when the baby makes those funny milk-drunk faces... I do chuckle. But it feels kind of muted? Like I'm not getting that same *gut* laugh I used to before she was born. Most of the time I'm just too tired to find things funny. So... "sometimes" would be about right.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*gives a small, tired nod*

Yeah… sometimes. Not like before, but every now and then something will catch me off-guard and I’ll laugh—just not as loud or as long.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*hesitates, smoothing the fabric of my leggings*

I try to… I’ll think, “Maybe tomorrow I’ll feel like going for coffee,” but when the time comes it just feels like one more thing. I still plan little outings, yet the excitement isn’t really there—more like I’m going through the motions. So, “not often” fits, I guess.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*quiet shrug*

Sometimes. Like, if she won’t settle at night, I’ll catch myself thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or I didn’t swaddle her tight enough. It’s usually little stuff—no big disasters—but yeah, I do wonder if I messed up somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*twists the edge of my sleeve*

Yeah... pretty often. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly wonder if she’s breathing okay, or I’ll lie down and my mind races about whether she’s too hot, too cold, if I sterilised the bottles right... There’s no real reason, but the worry just pops up. Most days, really.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*pulls cardigan tighter across my chest*

I... I get these waves, mostly in the evenings. My heart starts racing and I feel shaky, like something awful is about to happen—even though she’s right there in the bassinet, perfectly fine. It passes after a few minutes, but yes, it’s been happening several nights this week. So “yes, quite a lot.”
Things have been getting on top of me

*lets out a long, shaky breath*

Yeah... most days it feels like the dishes, the laundry, the constant feeding and burping just pile up faster than I can handle. I’ll finally finish one thing and three more appear. It’s not that I can’t do any of it—it’s just that it never lets up, so “yes, most of the time” is about right.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*looks down at the dark half-moons under my eyes*

I thought the sleep trouble was just from her night feeds, but even when she’s out I lie there staring at the ceiling, mind racing... replaying every little thing I did that day, worrying about tomorrow. I wouldn’t say I’m “so unhappy,” more keyed-up and weepy, but yes—most nights it takes me ages to drift off. So “yes, most of the time.”
I have felt sad or miserable

*shrugs one shoulder, eyes glassy*

Yeah… I do feel pretty low a lot of the time. Not every single moment—there are little bright spots—but most days there’s this gray cloud hanging around. So “yes, most of the time.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*shakes head quickly*

No, not like that. I might get watery-eyed when I’m really tired or overwhelmed, but I haven’t sat down and sobbed. Crying’s been pretty rare—so “no, never.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*looks up, eyes widening*

No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that laughter comes only sometimes and feels muted, that planning a simple outing feels like one more chore, and that a cloud of low mood hangs over most days. <quote>Most nights</quote> your mind races with worries about your baby's safety, and <quote>several nights this week</quote> sudden waves of panic leave you shaky and wide-eyed. Yet you continue to show up, pushing through dishes and feeds that <quote>never let up</quote>, and you clearly stated you have never thought of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes diminished anticipation and excitement, planning outings only out of obligation—closest to "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blaming "some of the time" for minor infant-care issues, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, unprovoked worries occurring "pretty often" and "most days," aligning with "Yes, very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple episodes of intense unexplained panic with racing heart, shakiness, and dread, explicitly stating "yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>She affirms frequent overwhelm and describes daily tasks piling up faster than she can manage, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly confirms "yes—most nights" and describes insomnia with racing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "yes, most of the time" and describes pervasive low mood</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 19 exceeds the ≥14 threshold that indicates probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. The patient endorses core symptoms: <sym>depressed mood</sym> most days (<quote>gray cloud</quote>), <sym>diminished interest</sym> (<quote>going through the motions</quote>), <sym>fatigue</sym> (<quote>too tired to find things funny</quote>), <sym>guilt</sym> (<quote>maybe I messed up</quote>), <sym>sleep disruption</sym> unrelated to infant care, and <sym>anxiety</sym> with multiple panic attacks. These meet DSM-5 criteria when combined with clinically observed distress and functional difficulty managing household tasks. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care physician</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within one week
2. Begin daily mood and anxiety self-rating to track severity and patterns
3. Plan brief respite: enlist partner, family, or friend to handle one night feeding or household block so you can obtain 4-5 hours of uninterrupted rest
4. Practice 5-minute paced breathing or grounding exercise whenever panic wave begins; keep a card with steps on night-stand
5. Limit information overload: choose one trusted parenting resource and mute anxiety-provoking social media accounts
6. Consider evidence-based treatments your doctor may offer-<med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or compatible <med>serotonergic antidepressants</med>-and discuss benefits/risks for breastfeeding
7. Schedule 2-week follow-up to re-screen with EPDS and adjust supports as needed
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Professional Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms endorsed (patient’s words paraphrased):
- Marked anhedonia: laughs “not as loud or as long”; anticipates outings “through the motions”  
- Persistent low mood: “pretty low a lot of the time… gray cloud most days”  
- Excessive guilt: self-blame for infant’s minor difficulties (“maybe I ate something…”)  
- Clinically significant anxiety: daily “mind races” about baby’s safety; repeated nocturnal panic episodes (“heart racing… shaky… several nights this week”)  
- Subjective overwhelm: “never lets up… most of the time”  
- Sleep disturbance attributed to racing thoughts, not solely infant care demands  
- Crying: watery-eyed when tired; denies sustained crying spells  
- Denies any self-harm ideation.

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days” for ≥2 weeks; functional impact evident in household tasks and emotional availability.

Screening significance: High endorsement of depressive (mood, anhedonia, guilt) and anxiety (persistent worry, panic) items consistent with possible perinatal depression ± anxiety; no current safety concerns.

Risk factors noted: first-time motherhood, sleep deprivation, lack of enjoyment, frequent panic symptoms.

Plan: Continue standardized assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7); discuss supports, psycho-education, and consider referral to perinatal mental-health specialty for further evaluation.
